subject: history
title: Interwar Britain: Suffrage, Strikes and Slump
welcome_lead: From the 1918 Representation of the People Act to the Depression of the 1930s.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on suffrage 1918/1928, the General Strike 1926 and the Great Depression in Britain.
final_note: You can analyse how WWI reshaped politics, economy and society.

concepts.def: Extended the franchise to all men aged 21+ and to women over 30 meeting a property qualification.
Lowered women's voting age to 21, achieving universal adult suffrage on equal terms.
Nine-day TUC sympathy strike (3-12 May 1926) in support of locked-out miners; collapsed without concessions.
1929-c.1933 slump: unemployment peaked at 22% (1932); industrial regions (Jarrow, South Wales) hardest hit.
Cross-party coalition under Ramsay MacDonald formed 24 August 1931 in response to the financial crisis.
200-strong march from Jarrow to London (5-31 October 1936) protesting unemployment in the North East.

walkthroughs.body_html: The 1918 Act tripled the electorate to 21 million. Lloyd George's coalition won the December 1918 'Khaki Election'. Labour overtook the Liberals: the first Labour government under MacDonald held office in 1924, falling over the Campbell Case and Zinoviev Letter.

The return to gold (1925) under Churchill overvalued sterling, hurting exports. The Samuel Commission recommended wage cuts in mining; the General Strike followed (3-12 May 1926). The Trade Disputes Act (1927) curbed union power. The Wall Street Crash hit British exports; unemployment exceeded 2.5 million by 1932. The May Report and August 1931 crisis broke the Labour government, producing the National Government.

Cheap money, the 1932 Import Duties Act and rearmament aided the Midlands and South East (new industries, suburban housing). Yet 'Special Areas' (1934 Act) suffered enduring unemployment. The Jarrow Crusade dramatised regional inequality. The 1936 abdication crisis briefly distracted; appeasement and rearmament dominated the late 1930s.
